name: scriptisto
desc: Language-agnostic "shebang interpreter" to write scripts in compiled languages
why: Lets you write shebang scripts in compiled languages, a neat trick that shows how interpreters work.

brief.what_it_is: Scriptisto is a command-line tool that acts as a shebang interpreter for single-file scripts written in compiled languages. You put a #!/usr/bin/env scriptisto line at the top of a source file, and the build steps go in a comment block between scriptisto-begin and scriptisto-end markers. On first run it builds the script, caches the result, and runs the binary. It takes a source file as input and produces a cached compiled executable, with no separate build step for the user. The README says templates exist for languages such as Rust, Go, C, Fortran, COBOL and C#.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is a tool for writing one-file scripts in languages that need compilation, dependency fetching or preprocessing, which otherwise need a separate build setup. The wiki 'Advantages' page is linked for more on use cases, but I did not fetch it.
brief.how_it_works: Scriptisto reads the build instructions (such as script_src and build_cmd) from comments in the script. If the script has changed, it rebuilds and caches the result. If a built copy already exists, it hands off to that binary with, per the README, under 1 ms of overhead. Builds can also run inside Docker so no compiler needs to be installed on the host.

brief.install_notes: The README says scriptisto ships as a prebuilt statically linked standalone binary on the GitHub Releases page, and as a crate on Crates.io (cargo install scriptisto would fetch it). Distribution packages are tracked on Repology. The README points to a wiki Installation page for details, which I did not fetch. Language toolchains are needed only for the languages you use: the C demo needs clang, GLib and pkg-config, and Docker is needed only if you choose Docker builds.
brief.standout: It is a shebang line that lets you run compiled-language source files directly, with build instructions kept inside the file as comments and results cached. Its own README calls the trick a way to see how interpreters work, which is the hook the scout notes picked up.
brief.status: Maintained. The Releases page shows v2.2.0 as Latest, dated 08 Jun (the year is not visible in the fetched text), with changelog entries for new Cobol and C# templates and a removed scrawl dependency. Earlier releases run from v0.6.10 through v2.1.1 in 2025 or earlier, with a v2.1.0 and v2.1.1 pair dated 10 Apr. The README has Travis-style build badges and a Repology packaging badge, but no explicit maintenance statement.
brief.caveats: The README's demo is a little confusing: it calls the source script.c and then says to run ./script.c, while the build_cmd writes a binary named ./script, so read the example carefully before copying it. Some templates, such as rust, can take a long time on the first build, and build logs are suppressed by default, so there may be no output for a while. The demo needs clang, GLib and pkg-config on the host. The README disclaimer says it is 'not an officially supported Google product'. The license is shown only as a badge with no text in the fetched README, so I could not confirm it.
quotes: It works as a "shebang" for those scripts, extracting build instructions from comments.
If a script was already built, scriptisto immediately delegates to a binary with only <1 ms overhead.
It is tool to enable writing one file scripts in languages that require compilation, dependencies fetching or preprocessing.
